threads.body: This replaces every `CompositeMeterRegistry` bean, including user-defined subclasses and composites that do not contain the OTel registry. Because the replacement is only an anonymous base `CompositeMeterRegistry`, a bean declared or injected by its concrete subtype will become a different runtime type and can fail with `BeanNotOfRequiredTypeException`. Restrict the post-processor to the Boot-managed composite that needs reordering, or use an approach that preserves the original bean's assignability and behavior.

replies.body:
Addressed in 9a8f99e3f0be83fa3c03dcf58997e01e36770898.

Analysis: Restrict replacement to Spring Boot's named auto-configured composite containing the OpenTelemetry registry. The wrapper delegates membership mutations to the original composite and computes a fresh ordered, unmodifiable registry snapshot for every read, preserving live membership and metric propagation.

Upsides: User-defined composite beans retain their concrete type and identity; supported add/remove operations remain visible to MetricsEndpoint; OpenTelemetry remains ordered last across Spring Boot 2 through 4.

Downsides: Each getRegistries() call allocates and sorts a small snapshot; identifying Boot's package-private implementation relies on its stable bean and simple class names.

threads.body: This captured set immediately becomes stale if either composite is changed through the supported `add`/`remove` API. The exposed wrapper still accepts those operations, but `getRegistries()` continues returning the initialization-time members, so `MetricsEndpoint` can omit a newly added registry or continue reading a removed one. Return a dynamically sorted, unmodifiable view of the current registry hierarchy, or keep this ordered view synchronized with membership changes.

threads.body: `CompositeMeterRegistry.add` normally rejects itself (and composites containing itself) to prevent cycles. Delegating directly to `original` bypasses that check because this wrapper's `getRegistries()` hides `original`; calling `meterRegistry.add(meterRegistry)` therefore creates a parent cycle and recurses until `StackOverflowError`. Reapply the cycle check before delegation.

replies.body:
Addressed in b2d5004166ce70c6bbe6dd41caee8e3c0fbf3cc9.

Analysis: Delegating add operations must retain the wrapper-level cycle guard that CompositeMeterRegistry normally applies. Recursively inspect a candidate composite hierarchy for the wrapper before delegating membership changes to the original registry.

Upsides: Self-addition and indirect parent cycles fail immediately with IllegalArgumentException instead of creating recursive registry graphs and eventual StackOverflowError.

Downsides: Composite additions perform an extra traversal of the candidate registry hierarchy.

threads.body: Spring Boot's `MeterRegistryPostProcessor` has already processed `original` and defers all `MeterBinder` binding against that instance. Returning a fresh composite here creates separate meter state: binders later add meters to `original`, and Micrometer does not propagate child meter creation back into this parent wrapper. As a result, the injected primary registry's normal `getMeters()`/`find(...)` APIs omit auto-bound metrics, even though `MetricsEndpoint` happens to work through the overridden `getRegistries()`. Please avoid replacing the bean with an independent registry, or make the replacement fully expose/delegate the original meter state.

replies.body:
Addressed in d217bd20cbfa1cbafa553068dd9af0c5be71dc88.

Analysis: Make the ordered postprocessor PriorityOrdered and expose its concrete return type so Spring runs it before Boot's registry postprocessor. Boot 2 and 3 then bind meters to the replacement itself. Boot 4 only recognizes its package-private auto-configured subtype for binding, so the replacement defers and applies Boot 4 MeterBinders after singleton initialization.

Upsides: Auto-bound meters live in the injected primary registry and remain available through getMeters() and find(...), while registry ordering and exporter propagation remain intact across Spring Boot 2 through 4.

Downsides: Spring Boot 4 binder application is explicitly mirrored because Boot's bindability check cannot recognize the replacement subtype.
